title: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
creator: Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman
summary: The paper that founded behavioural economics, still short and readable fifty years on. Tversky and Kahneman argue that people estimate probabilities not by any statistical procedure but by a small number of mental shortcuts, which usually work and fail in predictable ways. Representativeness judges how likely something is by how much it resembles a stereotype, which leads people to ignore base rates, sample size, and the fact that a conjunction cannot be more probable than its parts. Availability judges frequency by how easily examples come to mind, so vivid or recent events are overweighted. Anchoring starts from an arbitrary initial value and adjusts insufficiently, which the authors demonstrate by spinning a wheel of fortune before asking an unrelated numerical question. Each bias is illustrated with a compact experiment, and the closing argument is that these errors persist in experts and are not merely the result of carelessness or motivation.

title: Why Procrastinators Procrastinate
creator: Tim Urban
summary: Urban's cartoon model of procrastination is funnier than the research literature and closer to the experience than most of it. In the non-procrastinator's head a Rational Decision-Maker is in charge. In the procrastinator's head the same character shares the controls with an Instant Gratification Monkey, who has no concept of the future and steers toward whatever is easy and fun right now, landing them in the Dark Playground, where leisure is contaminated by guilt and produces no actual rest. The only thing the Monkey fears is the Panic Monster, which wakes near a deadline and briefly restores sane behaviour. The framework explains why procrastinators are not lazy, why the resulting work is rushed rather than absent, and why the truly damaging cases are the ones with no deadline at all, such as starting a business, ending a relationship, or getting fit, where the Panic Monster never arrives.

title: Forget About Setting Goals. Focus on This Instead.
creator: James Clear
summary: Clear separates goals, the results you want, from systems, the processes that produce them, and argues that the second does nearly all the work. A coach's goal is a championship; the system is how they recruit and run practice. He then gives four reasons to concentrate on systems. Winners and losers share the same goals, so the goal cannot be what distinguishes them. Achieving a goal is only a momentary change, and treating the symptom without fixing the process means the problem returns, as it does for people who tidy a messy room without changing the habits that made it messy. Goals restrict happiness by postponing satisfaction until a threshold is crossed, and they encourage the assumption that you will be content once you get there. Finally, goals are at odds with long-term progress, because people often stop after reaching them; a system is something you keep running.

title: Self-Determination Theory: an overview
creator: Richard Ryan and Edward Deci (center for SDT)
summary: The canonical overview of Self-Determination Theory, written by the researchers who developed it. The starting point is that motivation is not a single quantity to be raised or lowered but has different kinds, which differ in quality and in what they predict. The theory distinguishes intrinsic motivation, doing something because it is interesting in itself, from a spectrum of extrinsic motivations that range from purely externally controlled through to fully internalised values. Which of these operates depends on whether three basic psychological needs are supported: competence, autonomy, and relatedness. Environments that satisfy those needs produce better persistence, creativity, and wellbeing; environments that thwart them, including some reward and evaluation systems, can undermine motivation that was already present. The page summarises the sub-theories and the decades of experimental and field research behind them, in education, work, sport, healthcare, and psychotherapy.

title: RSA ANIMATE: Drive, the surprising truth about what motivates us
creator: Daniel Pink
summary: An illustrated condensation of Pink's talk on motivation research, drawn live as he speaks. He begins with experiments, several funded by the Federal Reserve and run by economists at MIT and in Madurai, India, in which people were offered small, medium, and large bonuses for a range of tasks. As long as the task involved only mechanical skill, larger rewards produced better performance. As soon as it required even rudimentary cognitive skill, larger rewards produced worse performance. Pink argues that this result, uncomfortable for both economics and management practice, means money works as a motivator only up to the point where pay is no longer a concern. Beyond it, performance depends on autonomy, mastery, and purpose. He illustrates with Atlassian's engineering days, Google's twenty percent time, and Wikipedia, and notes the gap between what science knows and what business does.

title: Augmenting Long-term Memory
creator: Michael Nielsen
summary: Nielsen opens with Solomon Shereshevsky, the Moscow journalist whose memory Alexander Luria studied for thirty years and could find no limit to, then turns to how ordinary people can build reliable long-term memory using spaced repetition software. The essay is both a practical manual and an argument. Practically, he explains how he uses Anki to read research papers in unfamiliar fields, how to write good cards, why cards should be atomic, why you should not add cards about things you do not care about, and how the time cost works out over a lifetime of reviews. The argument is that memory is not a low-grade substitute for understanding but a precondition for it: fluency with a field's facts is what allows chunking, pattern recognition, and creative connection. He also reflects on the personal experience of the practice, including its failure modes and the strange feeling of trusting a system with your own recall.

title: Spaced Repetition for Efficient Learning
creator: Gwern Branwen
summary: A long literature review of the spacing effect and of the software built on it. The core finding, replicated for over a century, is that reviews spread out over increasing intervals produce far more durable memory than the same total time spent cramming, and the review essay traces the experimental history behind that claim. Branwen then does the arithmetic that most enthusiasts skip: how many minutes a card actually costs over a lifetime, at what point that investment pays for itself, and therefore which facts are worth adding and which are not. He is candid about the limits, including the difficulty of making cards for conceptual rather than factual material, the risk of accumulating a collection you will not maintain, and the evidence on whether the technique transfers to real academic performance. Extensive citations make it a good entry point into the underlying research rather than a closed argument.

title: Learn how to Study Using Retrieval Practice
creator: Megan Smith and Yana Weinstein
summary: A short, practical explanation of the single most robust finding in the science of studying, written by two cognitive psychologists for students. Retrieval practice means bringing information back to mind from memory rather than reviewing it in front of you, and the timing matters: you need to have forgotten a little for the retrieval to do any work, which is why re-reading immediately after a lecture feels productive and is not. The post explains why the technique feels harder and less effective than highlighting or re-reading even though it produces substantially better retention, describes concrete ways to do it, including free recall onto a blank page, flashcards used properly, and writing your own practice questions, and stresses checking your answers afterwards. It is deliberately brief and links to the underlying studies, making it a good first thing to send to someone who studies by highlighting.

title: How To Remember Anything Forever-ish
creator: Nicky Case
summary: An interactive comic about spaced repetition that you play as much as read. Case starts with the observation that lectures, cramming, and re-reading are both boring and ineffective, then introduces the memory card game he used to learn more French vocabulary in two months than in two years of school. The comic walks through the forgetting curve, why testing yourself beats reviewing, and how increasing intervals keep material just on the edge of recall, using small playable widgets rather than diagrams so the reader experiences forgetting and retrieval while reading. Later sections cover what the technique is and is not good for, how to write cards that are not useless, and how to fit the practice into a day. There is a section aimed at teachers, a full source list at the end, and the whole thing is free, open source, and unusually honest about limitations.

title: The Feynman Technique: The Ultimate Guide to Learning Anything Faster
creator: Farnam Street
summary: A compact guide to a four-step learning method attributed to the physicist Richard Feynman, whose insight was that complexity and jargon usually conceal a lack of understanding. Step one is to pick a concept and write everything you know about it on a blank page, adding to it in a different colour as you learn more. Step two is to explain it as you would to a twelve-year-old, using plain words and short sentences, because simple language forces you to actually understand rather than recite. Step three is to review what you could not explain, return to the source material, and fill the gaps that the explanation exposed. Step four is to test the explanation on someone else and refine it based on where their questions land. The article makes the case that the technique works because it converts passive familiarity into the harder task of production, and that the gaps it reveals are the point.

title: Learning how to learn
creator: Barbara Oakley
summary: Oakley failed her way through school mathematics and science and is now a professor of engineering, and the talk explains what she changed. The central idea is that the brain has two modes. Focused mode is deliberate, narrow attention on material you already partly understand. Diffuse mode is the relaxed, wandering state that appears while walking, showering, or falling asleep, and it is the one that makes connections between distant ideas. Learning something difficult requires alternating between them, which is why staring at a problem for hours fails and why breaks are not slacking. She covers how chunking builds expertise, why the feeling of fluency when re-reading is an illusion of competence, why practice testing works better, and how procrastination interacts with all of it. The examples come from her own retraining as an adult rather than from laboratory descriptions.

title: The Acceleration of Addictiveness
creator: Paul Graham
summary: Graham's 2010 essay makes one observation and follows it carefully. Hard liquor, cigarettes, heroin, and crack are all concentrated forms of less addictive predecessors, and the process that concentrates them is the same technological progress that cures diseases. Making things do more of what we want is good when we want to want it and bad when it turns opium into heroin, but there is no way to have one without the other, and the process is accelerating. The consequence is that an increasing number of ordinary things will become things we like too much, from food to television to online life, faster than social custom can develop defences against them. He argues that society's antibodies to new addictions take generations to form, that in the interim the burden falls on individuals, and that the people who cope will look eccentric, since avoiding what everyone else consumes normally does.

title: On Digital Minimalism
creator: Cal Newport
summary: Newport, a computer scientist who is optimistic about computing and indifferent to his smartphone, sets out the philosophy behind that apparent contradiction. He borrows from the minimalism movement, where the point is not owning less for its own sake but refusing to let possessions accumulate unexamined, and applies the same standard to digital tools. Digital minimalism treats each app, service, and account as something that must justify itself against a clearly identified value, and holds that a tool is only worth adopting if it is the best available way to serve that value, not merely if it offers some benefit. That last clause does most of the work, since almost any service offers some benefit, which is how people end up with dozens of them. The piece is an early, tentative statement of ideas Newport later developed into a book, and it reads as thinking in progress.

title: How I Got My Attention Back
creator: Craig Mod
summary: Mod spent twenty-eight days on the grounds of an old estate in central Virginia with no internet, and writes about what came back. The essay opens with the observation that there are a thousand beautiful ways to start a day that do not begin with looking at a phone, and that almost nobody chooses one. Cutting the connection was not an escape from the real world so much as an experiment in whether he could still sit quietly alone, in Pascal's sense. What he describes is not instant clarity but a slow return: attention lengthening over days, the compulsion to check fading, reading becoming possible again at book length rather than in fragments. He is honest that the residency was an artificial condition and that the difficult part is carrying anything back, and the later sections deal with the compromises and tools he adopted afterwards rather than prescribing abstinence.
